implementation_notes: Lambda expressions (Java 8) capture effectively-final locals - a captured variable must never be reassigned, which removes the late-binding class of bug by construction. To keep mutable state in a closure, hold a mutable object (an AtomicLong, a List, a one-element array) rather than the variable. Java's lambdas are objects and are stateless unless they capture; the JVM implements them via invokedynamic and LambdaMetafactory, which spin the class once per call site, not per instance. Anonymous inner classes are the pre-8 form and do capture mutable locals, so a codebase can contain both semantics at once.
idiom_name: lambda expression capturing effectively-final locals; anonymous inner class for mutable capture
pitfalls: Capturing a mutable object to work around effectively-final is correct but hides the state; name the object for what it is (a counter, a buffer) rather than 'state'.
A lambda capturing this inside a listener registered on the same object keeps the object reachable for as long as the listener lives.

The effectively-final rule is per-variable, so a mutable holder compiles while an accidental capture of a reassigned local fails loudly - do not route around the compiler with holders for non-state reasons.
